learningObjectives.title: Changes of state and the particle model

questions.q: Which equation correctly gives the density of a substance?
questions.explain: Density is defined as mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of density?
questions.explain: In SI base units density is measured in kilograms per cubic metre.

questions.q: A change of state, such as melting or boiling, is best described as which kind of change?
questions.explain: Changes of state are physical changes because no new substance is formed and they are reversible.

questions.q: Why is mass conserved when a substance changes state?
options: The number of particles stays the same
questions.explain: No particles are created or destroyed during a change of state, so the total mass is unchanged.

questions.q: According to the particle model, how are the particles in a gas arranged and moving?
options: Far apart, randomly arranged and moving quickly
Close together in a fixed regular pattern
Close together but able to slide past each other
Far apart but held in fixed positions
questions.explain: Gas particles are widely spaced, random in arrangement and move rapidly in all directions.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from a solid to a liquid?
questions.explain: Melting is the change from solid to liquid as the substance is heated.

questions.q: Why is a substance usually much less dense as a gas than as a solid?
options: Its particles are much further apart as a gas
Its particles become lighter as a gas
Its particles are destroyed when it becomes a gas
Its particles get larger as a gas
questions.explain: The same mass of particles occupies a far larger volume as a gas, so density is much lower.

questions.q: A block has a mass of 6 kg and a volume of 0.002 m³. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass ÷ volume = 6 ÷ 0.002 = 3000 kg/m³.

questions.q: What is meant by the internal energy of a system?
options: The total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles
Only the kinetic energy of its particles
The energy stored in the bonds between molecules only
The heat supplied to it from outside
questions.explain: Internal energy is the total of the kinetic and potential energies stored in a system's particles.

questions.q: Which equation links the change in thermal energy to specific heat capacity?
questions.explain: Change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.

questions.q: Which equation gives the energy needed for a change of state using specific latent heat?
questions.explain: Energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat.

questions.q: Why does the temperature stay constant while a pure substance is changing state?
options: The energy is used to change the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy
No energy is being supplied during the change
The particles stop moving during the change
The specific heat capacity becomes zero
questions.explain: During a change of state the supplied energy alters bonds (potential energy) rather than raising particle kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.

questions.q: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to do what?
options: Raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C
Melt 1 kg of the substance completely
Raise the temperature of any mass by 1 °C
Boil 1 kg of the substance completely
questions.explain: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C (or 1 K).

questions.q: How much thermal energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water (specific heat capacity 4200 J/kg °C) by 10 °C?
How much energy is required to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C, given the specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 334 000 J/kg?
The specific latent heat of fusion refers to which change of state?
questions.explain: Latent heat of fusion is the energy to change state between solid and liquid, i.e. melting or freezing.

questions.q: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?
options: Particles colliding with the walls of the container
Particles being pulled towards the walls
The weight of the gas particles
The particles sticking to the walls
questions.explain: Gas pressure arises from the many collisions of fast-moving particles with the container walls.

questions.q: When a gas in a sealed rigid container is heated, its pressure increases. Why?
options: The particles move faster and collide with the walls more often and harder
There are more particles in the container
questions.explain: Higher temperature raises particle kinetic energy, so collisions with the walls become more frequent and forceful, increasing pressure.

questions.q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, which quantity stays constant?
questions.explain: At constant temperature for a fixed mass of gas, pressure × volume (pV) is constant.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has its volume halved. What happens to its pressure?
questions.explain: Because pV is constant at constant temperature, halving the volume doubles the pressure.
